shortDefinition: A technique that targets Kerberos service tickets associated with service accounts so password material can be attacked offline.
simpleExplanation: An attacker requests a Kerberos service ticket for an account that runs a service. The ticket can then be analysed offline in an attempt to recover the service account password.
technicalExplanation: Kerberoasting abuses the fact that domain users can request service tickets for SPN-backed service accounts. The encrypted portion of the ticket is derived from the service account secret, enabling offline password guessing without repeatedly contacting the domain controller.
offensiveRelevance: Used during Active Directory assessments to identify weak service-account passwords and paths to privilege escalation.
defensiveRelevance: Use strong managed service-account passwords, prefer gMSA where possible, monitor unusual service-ticket activity and reduce unnecessary service-account privilege.

shortDefinition: Server-Side Request Forgery causes a server to make unintended requests to internal or external resources.
simpleExplanation: Instead of the attacker directly contacting a target, a vulnerable application is tricked into making the request for them.
technicalExplanation: SSRF commonly appears in URL fetchers, webhook handlers, import features and proxy-style functionality. It can expose internal services, cloud metadata endpoints or trust boundaries unreachable from the internet.
offensiveRelevance: Useful for validating server-side trust boundaries and internal network exposure during authorised web assessments.
defensiveRelevance: Apply strict allowlists, URL parsing controls, outbound network restrictions and metadata-service protections.

shortDefinition: An authentication technique that uses an NTLM password hash instead of the plaintext password.
simpleExplanation: If an attacker obtains a reusable NTLM hash, some Windows authentication flows may accept it without requiring the original password.
technicalExplanation: Pass-the-Hash leverages NTLM authentication material as a reusable credential for compatible services and protocols. Its practical impact depends on network reachability, account privileges and defensive controls.
offensiveRelevance: Used to validate credential reuse and lateral-movement risk in Windows environments.
defensiveRelevance: Reduce NTLM usage, segment administration, use privileged access controls and monitor unusual remote-authentication patterns.

shortDefinition: An authorisation framework that lets applications obtain delegated access to resources without sharing a user's password.
simpleExplanation: OAuth lets one service grant another service limited access on behalf of a user.
technicalExplanation: OAuth 2.0 defines roles and flows for delegated authorisation using access tokens. Security depends heavily on correct redirect URI validation, state handling, token storage, client configuration and scope design.
offensiveRelevance: Reviewed during application assessments for redirect, token, scope and client-security weaknesses.
defensiveRelevance: Use exact redirect URI validation, PKCE where appropriate, least-privilege scopes and secure token handling.

shortDefinition: Endpoint Detection and Response monitors endpoint activity to detect, investigate and respond to suspicious behaviour.
simpleExplanation: EDR gives defenders visibility into what is happening on laptops and servers and helps them respond to suspicious activity.
technicalExplanation: EDR platforms collect process, file, registry, network and identity telemetry. They generate detections and may provide isolation, investigation and remediation capabilities.
offensiveRelevance: Security assessments often validate whether realistic behaviours are detected or blocked by endpoint controls.
defensiveRelevance: EDR provides high-value endpoint visibility, behavioural detection and response functions.

shortDefinition: A knowledge base that maps real-world adversary tactics and techniques.
simpleExplanation: ATT&CK gives security teams a shared language for describing attacker behaviour.
technicalExplanation: MITRE ATT&CK organises behaviours into tactics, techniques and sub-techniques and is widely used for adversary emulation, detection engineering and gap analysis.
offensiveRelevance: Red and purple teams map simulated behaviours to ATT&CK to make exercises structured and comparable.
defensiveRelevance: Blue teams use ATT&CK to organise detections, hunts and coverage assessments.

shortDefinition: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures is a standardised identifier system for publicly disclosed security vulnerabilities.
simpleExplanation: A CVE number gives a public vulnerability a common name that vendors, researchers and defenders can reference.
technicalExplanation: CVE records identify publicly disclosed vulnerabilities and are often enriched by vendor advisories, NVD entries and scoring systems such as CVSS.
offensiveRelevance: Helps testers correlate known vulnerabilities with affected products and versions.
defensiveRelevance: Supports vulnerability management, patch prioritisation and asset exposure tracking.

shortDefinition: A technique that abuses Windows DLL search behaviour so a malicious library is loaded instead of the intended one.
simpleExplanation: If an application looks for a DLL in an unsafe location first, an attacker may be able to place a different DLL there.
technicalExplanation: DLL hijacking depends on search order, writable paths, missing libraries, application loading behaviour and trust controls such as WDAC or AppLocker.
offensiveRelevance: Used to validate unsafe DLL loading and privilege boundaries in Windows assessments.
defensiveRelevance: Harden search paths, remove writable trusted paths and enforce application control.

shortDefinition: The process of gaining higher privileges than those initially available.
simpleExplanation: An attacker begins with limited access and finds a way to become administrator, root or another more privileged identity.
technicalExplanation: Privilege escalation can result from vulnerable software, weak permissions, exposed credentials, unsafe services, token abuse or misconfigured trust relationships.
offensiveRelevance: Privilege escalation is a core assessment area after initial access.
defensiveRelevance: Defenders reduce risk through least privilege, patching, secure configuration and monitoring sensitive privilege changes.

shortDefinition: A class of attacks that manipulates an AI system's instructions through attacker-controlled input.
simpleExplanation: A user or external source gives an AI system instructions that conflict with the developer's intended behaviour.
technicalExplanation: Prompt injection can be direct or indirect and becomes especially relevant when LLMs can access tools, retrieve external content, call APIs or act autonomously.
offensiveRelevance: Used to test instruction hierarchy, data boundaries, tool access and agentic behaviour.
defensiveRelevance: Apply least privilege, isolate tools, validate outputs, constrain retrieval and test against adversarial inputs.

shortDefinition: An identity layer built on top of OAuth 2.0 that provides authentication and identity claims.
simpleExplanation: OIDC lets an application confirm who a user is while OAuth handles delegated access.
technicalExplanation: OIDC introduces ID tokens, discovery, userinfo endpoints, claims and defined authentication flows on top of OAuth 2.0.
offensiveRelevance: Assessed for issuer validation, redirect handling, token validation and client misconfiguration.
defensiveRelevance: Validate signatures, issuer, audience, nonce and redirect URI behaviour.

shortDefinition: JSON Web Token is a compact format for transmitting signed or encrypted claims between parties.
simpleExplanation: A JWT is a structured token commonly used to carry identity or authorisation information.
technicalExplanation: JWT security depends on correct algorithm selection, signature validation, key management, claim validation and token lifecycle handling.
offensiveRelevance: Reviewed for weak signature validation, claim manipulation and key confusion issues.
defensiveRelevance: Pin algorithms, validate claims and protect signing keys.

shortDefinition: A web vulnerability that allows attacker-controlled script to execute in another user's browser.
simpleExplanation: An application places unsafe user input into a web page and the browser treats it as executable code.
technicalExplanation: XSS appears as reflected, stored or DOM-based behaviour depending on the injection and execution context.
offensiveRelevance: Used to test output encoding, sanitisation and client-side trust boundaries.
defensiveRelevance: Apply contextual encoding, safe DOM APIs, sanitisation and CSP as defence in depth.

shortDefinition: An Active Directory technique that abuses directory replication rights to request credential data from a domain controller.
simpleExplanation: An account with powerful replication permissions can ask a domain controller for password-related data as if it were another domain controller.
technicalExplanation: DCSync abuses directory replication APIs and requires specific replication rights. It is powerful because it can expose credential material without reading the domain-controller database directly.
offensiveRelevance: Used to validate highly privileged directory permissions and compromise paths.
defensiveRelevance: Audit replication rights, minimise privileged groups and monitor unusual replication requests.

shortDefinition: A forged Kerberos Ticket Granting Ticket created using the KRBTGT account secret.
simpleExplanation: If an attacker has the KRBTGT secret, they can create Kerberos tickets that appear to come from the domain.
technicalExplanation: Golden Ticket attacks rely on possession of the KRBTGT key material and permit highly privileged forged TGTs within the affected domain.
offensiveRelevance: Used to demonstrate impact after deep Active Directory compromise.
defensiveRelevance: Protect domain-controller secrets, rotate KRBTGT after compromise and monitor anomalous Kerberos behaviour.

shortDefinition: Windows Defender Application Control is a Windows application-control technology used to restrict which code can run.
simpleExplanation: WDAC lets organisations define which applications, scripts and code are trusted to execute.
technicalExplanation: WDAC policies can enforce signer, hash, path and reputation-based trust decisions and can be combined with other Windows security controls.
offensiveRelevance: Assessment focuses on whether execution controls match intended security policy and whether trusted paths introduce gaps.
defensiveRelevance: Use strong allow rules, minimise writable trusted paths and validate effective policy.

shortDefinition: A structured collaborative approach where offensive and defensive security teams work together to improve resilience.
simpleExplanation: Red and blue teams share what they are doing and what they observe so both sides learn and improve faster.
technicalExplanation: Purple teaming can combine adversary simulation, telemetry review, detection validation, feedback cycles and knowledge transfer.
offensiveRelevance: Provides rapid feedback on whether attack behaviours are realistic and observable.
defensiveRelevance: Improves detection engineering, response readiness and understanding of adversary behaviour.

shortDefinition: A protocol for connecting AI applications to tools, data sources and external capabilities through a standard interface.
simpleExplanation: MCP gives AI systems a common way to interact with tools and data.
technicalExplanation: MCP introduces new trust boundaries around tool permissions, server authenticity, data exposure and action approval.
offensiveRelevance: Security testing can evaluate tool abuse, over-privileged servers, prompt-driven action chains and data exposure.
defensiveRelevance: Use least privilege, explicit approvals, server trust controls and action auditing.

shortDefinition: An AI architecture that retrieves external information and supplies it to a language model as context.
simpleExplanation: RAG lets an AI model look up relevant information before answering.
technicalExplanation: RAG systems combine retrieval, ranking and generation. Security concerns include poisoned content, data leakage, access-control bypass and indirect prompt injection.
offensiveRelevance: Testers assess trust in retrieved content and separation between users, sources and actions.
defensiveRelevance: Enforce source permissions, provenance, retrieval filtering and prompt-injection resistance.

shortDefinition: Techniques used to move from one compromised system or identity to another within an environment.
simpleExplanation: After gaining access to one system, an attacker tries to reach other systems or accounts.
technicalExplanation: Lateral movement can use remote services, administrative tools, stolen credentials, trust relationships or exposed management interfaces.
offensiveRelevance: It validates segmentation, identity boundaries and remote-administration controls.
defensiveRelevance: Defenders limit lateral movement through segmentation, credential protection and monitoring remote access behaviour.

shortDefinition: A hands-on cybersecurity challenge format used to practise technical security skills in a controlled environment.
simpleExplanation: CTFs are security competitions or practice labs where participants solve challenges to find hidden flags. They are commonly used to learn web security, cryptography, forensics, reverse engineering, binary exploitation and other practical skills.
technicalExplanation: A Capture The Flag environment typically contains intentionally vulnerable systems, puzzles or challenge services. Players analyse the challenge, identify the weakness or intended technique and recover a flag string that proves completion.
offensiveRelevance: CTFs help security testers practise exploitation, enumeration, privilege escalation, reversing and problem-solving without targeting real production systems.
defensiveRelevance: Blue-team and incident-response CTFs can teach log analysis, threat hunting, forensics and detection engineering.

shortDefinition: Command and Control infrastructure is used to communicate with and manage systems under an operator's control during adversary simulations.
simpleExplanation: In red-team exercises, C2 is the communication layer between an operator and a controlled test system. It lets the operator issue tasks and receive results.
technicalExplanation: C2 frameworks provide tasking, session management, payload communications, transport profiles and operator workflows. Defenders study C2 patterns to identify suspicious network and endpoint behaviour.
offensiveRelevance: Red teams use C2 in authorised simulations to emulate how real adversaries maintain remote control after initial access.
defensiveRelevance: Defenders monitor unusual outbound traffic, beaconing patterns, suspicious processes and anomalous protocol use associated with C2 activity.

shortDefinition: An offensive security team that simulates realistic adversary behaviour to test people, processes and technology.
simpleExplanation: A red team acts like an attacker in a controlled and authorised exercise. The goal is to test how well an organisation can prevent, detect and respond to realistic attacks.
technicalExplanation: Red-team engagements may combine initial access, privilege escalation, persistence, credential access, lateral movement and objective-based activity while following agreed rules of engagement.
offensiveRelevance: Red teaming validates realistic attack paths and operational security controls beyond isolated vulnerability testing.
defensiveRelevance: Findings reveal detection gaps, response weaknesses and opportunities to improve security architecture and monitoring.

shortDefinition: A defensive security team focused on preventing, detecting, investigating and responding to security threats.
simpleExplanation: The blue team protects systems and monitors for suspicious activity. It investigates alerts, contains incidents and improves defensive controls.
technicalExplanation: Blue-team work includes telemetry collection, detection engineering, endpoint and network monitoring, incident response, threat hunting and security hardening.
offensiveRelevance: Offensive teams rely on blue-team feedback to understand which behaviours were detected and how realistic attack simulations affected controls.
defensiveRelevance: Blue teams operate the defensive capabilities used to identify and contain attacker behaviour.

shortDefinition: A collaborative approach where offensive and defensive security teams work together to improve security outcomes.
simpleExplanation: Purple teaming brings red and blue teams together. Instead of working separately, they share what they are doing, what is detected and what needs improvement.
technicalExplanation: Purple-team exercises often combine attack simulation, telemetry review, detection validation, rapid feedback and knowledge transfer in short iterative cycles.
offensiveRelevance: Red-team techniques are used transparently to validate whether security controls observe and block realistic behaviour.
defensiveRelevance: Blue teams receive direct feedback that helps improve detections, response playbooks and control coverage.

shortDefinition: A Security Operations Center is the team and capability responsible for monitoring, triaging and responding to security events.
simpleExplanation: A SOC watches security alerts and investigates suspicious activity across an organisation.
technicalExplanation: SOC teams commonly use SIEM, EDR, network telemetry, threat intelligence and case-management systems to monitor events and coordinate incident response.
offensiveRelevance: Red and purple teams evaluate whether SOC processes detect simulated attacker activity and escalate incidents effectively.
defensiveRelevance: The SOC is a central operational function for detection, triage, escalation and coordinated response.

shortDefinition: A platform that centralises security logs and helps correlate, search and analyse events.
simpleExplanation: A SIEM collects logs from many systems so defenders can search them and detect suspicious patterns.
technicalExplanation: SIEM platforms ingest and normalise logs, support correlation rules, dashboards, alerts, threat hunting and investigation workflows.
offensiveRelevance: Purple teams can use SIEM visibility to confirm whether attack behaviours generated the expected telemetry.
defensiveRelevance: SIEM is a core detection and investigation capability for many SOC environments.

shortDefinition: Intelligence gathered from publicly available information sources.
simpleExplanation: OSINT means collecting useful information from public sources such as websites, documents, social media, DNS records and public databases.
technicalExplanation: OSINT workflows may combine search engines, certificate transparency, public code repositories, metadata, archives and public records to build context about an organisation or target.
offensiveRelevance: Authorised assessments use OSINT to understand exposed assets, technologies, people and infrastructure before deeper testing.
defensiveRelevance: Organisations use OSINT to understand their external exposure and identify information that may help attackers.

shortDefinition: A social-engineering technique that attempts to influence users into revealing information or performing an action.
simpleExplanation: Phishing usually uses deceptive email, messages or websites to persuade someone to click, log in, open a file or share sensitive information.
technicalExplanation: Phishing simulations may test awareness, mail controls, authentication workflows and detection capabilities under clearly authorised conditions.
offensiveRelevance: Red teams may emulate phishing to test initial-access resilience and human security controls.
defensiveRelevance: Defences include user awareness, MFA, email security, domain protection and detection of suspicious links and attachments.

shortDefinition: Methods used to maintain access to a system or environment over time.
simpleExplanation: Persistence is how an attacker tries to keep access even after a reboot, password change or temporary interruption.
technicalExplanation: Persistence can involve services, scheduled tasks, registry mechanisms, account changes, startup locations, cloud identities or other trusted execution paths.
offensiveRelevance: Authorised simulations test whether persistence activity is prevented or detected.
defensiveRelevance: Defenders monitor startup mechanisms, identity changes and unusual long-lived access patterns.

shortDefinition: Using one compromised or controlled host as a bridge to reach systems that are otherwise inaccessible.
simpleExplanation: A pivot lets an operator route traffic through one system to reach another network or service.
technicalExplanation: Pivoting may use tunnels, proxies, port forwarding or routing mechanisms to access internal systems through an authorised foothold.
offensiveRelevance: Used in controlled assessments to validate internal segmentation and reachability.
defensiveRelevance: Monitor unexpected tunnels, unusual routing behaviour and systems communicating across normally separated network zones.

shortDefinition: A way to describe how adversaries operate at strategic, technical and procedural levels.
simpleExplanation: TTPs describe what attackers try to achieve, how they do it and the procedures they follow.
technicalExplanation: Tactics represent objectives, techniques describe methods and procedures capture concrete implementations or observed behaviours.
offensiveRelevance: Red teams use TTPs to model realistic adversary behaviour.
defensiveRelevance: Defenders use TTPs to design detections, hunts and control validation.

shortDefinition: Observable data that may indicate malicious or suspicious activity.
simpleExplanation: An IoC can be something like a malicious IP address, file hash, domain or other artefact associated with suspicious activity.
technicalExplanation: Indicators are useful for enrichment and detection but can be fragile because adversaries can change infrastructure, files and domains quickly.
offensiveRelevance: Red teams may generate test indicators so defenders can validate telemetry and detection workflows.
defensiveRelevance: Defenders use IoCs for detection, blocking, hunting and incident scoping.

shortDefinition: A weakness in software, hardware, configuration or process that can be exploited to create security impact.
simpleExplanation: A vulnerability is a security weakness that can allow an attacker to do something they should not be able to do.
technicalExplanation: Vulnerabilities can arise from design flaws, implementation bugs, unsafe defaults, insecure configuration, trust failures or weak access controls.
offensiveRelevance: Penetration testers identify and validate vulnerabilities to demonstrate real-world risk.
defensiveRelevance: Organisations reduce exposure by patching, hardening, monitoring and prioritising remediation.

shortDefinition: Code, data or a technique that takes advantage of a vulnerability to achieve a security-relevant outcome.
simpleExplanation: An exploit is the method used to turn a vulnerability into an actual effect.
technicalExplanation: Exploitation can result in code execution, access-control bypass, information disclosure, privilege escalation or other impact depending on the vulnerability.
offensiveRelevance: Security testers use controlled exploitation to verify that a reported weakness is real and to understand its impact.
defensiveRelevance: Exploit awareness helps defenders prioritise remediation and validate compensating controls.

shortDefinition: The structured process of detecting, containing, eradicating and recovering from security incidents.
simpleExplanation: Incident response is how an organisation handles a security breach or serious security event.
technicalExplanation: Typical phases include preparation, detection and analysis, containment, eradication, recovery and lessons learned.
offensiveRelevance: Red-team and purple-team exercises can validate whether incident-response processes activate effectively.
defensiveRelevance: Incident response coordinates technical and organisational actions during security events.

shortDefinition: A proactive process for searching systems and data for hidden adversary activity that automated alerts may miss.
simpleExplanation: Threat hunting means actively looking for signs of malicious behaviour instead of waiting for an alert. Hunters form a hypothesis, search relevant telemetry, follow evidence and determine whether suspicious activity is present.
technicalExplanation: Threat hunting combines hypotheses, threat intelligence and telemetry from sources such as SIEM, EDR, endpoint logs and network traffic. Findings are validated, scoped and then converted into detections, response actions or further investigation.
offensiveRelevance: Understanding threat hunting helps offensive teams anticipate which behaviours defenders can discover even when no alert fires automatically.
defensiveRelevance: Threat hunting helps defenders uncover stealthy activity, validate assumptions, improve detections and reduce blind spots.

shortDefinition: A security model that assumes no implicit trust and continuously verifies users, devices and access requests.
simpleExplanation: Zero Trust follows the idea “never trust, always verify.” Access decisions consider identity, device health, context, least privilege and segmentation rather than trusting users simply because they are inside a network.
technicalExplanation: Zero Trust architectures continuously evaluate identity, device posture, policy, resource sensitivity and risk. Common principles include strong authentication, least privilege, micro-segmentation, continuous monitoring and adaptive access controls.
offensiveRelevance: For security testers, Zero Trust changes attack paths by reducing implicit network trust and requiring repeated identity and device validation.
defensiveRelevance: Zero Trust can reduce lateral movement, excessive privilege and the impact of compromised accounts or devices.

shortDefinition: Malicious software that encrypts data or disrupts systems and demands payment for recovery.
simpleExplanation: Ransomware is malware designed to make files or systems unavailable, often by encrypting them, and then demand payment. Modern incidents may also involve data theft and extortion.
technicalExplanation: A ransomware incident can involve initial access, privilege escalation, credential theft, lateral movement, defence evasion, data exfiltration and mass encryption. Effective response focuses on containment, evidence preservation, recovery and closing the original access path.
offensiveRelevance: Adversary simulations may safely emulate ransomware behaviours without destructive encryption to test segmentation, detection and response readiness.
defensiveRelevance: Defenders reduce ransomware risk through strong identity controls, segmentation, endpoint protection, tested backups, rapid containment and incident-response preparation.

shortDefinition: An authentication approach that requires two or more factors to verify identity.
simpleExplanation: MFA requires more than one kind of proof when signing in, such as a password plus an authenticator app, hardware security key or biometric factor.
technicalExplanation: Authentication factors are commonly grouped into something you know, something you have and something you are. MFA reduces reliance on a single credential and can be combined with risk-based or step-up verification.
offensiveRelevance: During authorised assessments, MFA is evaluated for bypass opportunities, weak recovery paths, session handling and resistance to phishing or token theft.
defensiveRelevance: MFA significantly reduces account takeover risk when passwords are stolen, especially when phishing-resistant factors are used.

shortDefinition: A framework for delegated authorisation that lets applications obtain limited access to protected resources.
simpleExplanation: OAuth 2.0 allows a user to grant an application limited access without giving that application the user password.
technicalExplanation: OAuth 2.0 defines roles, grants and token flows between a resource owner, client, authorisation server and resource server. Access tokens represent delegated authorisation and are constrained by scopes, audience, lifetime and server policy.
offensiveRelevance: Security testing focuses on redirect URI validation, state and PKCE handling, token leakage, scope enforcement, client trust boundaries and implementation mistakes.
defensiveRelevance: Use strict redirect URI matching, PKCE where appropriate, short lived tokens, least privilege scopes, secure token storage and strong server side validation.

shortDefinition: An identity layer on OAuth 2.0 that allows applications to verify user identity using standardised tokens and claims.
simpleExplanation: OIDC adds authentication and identity information to OAuth 2.0 so an application can know who the user is.
technicalExplanation: OIDC introduces the ID token, UserInfo endpoint, discovery metadata and standard claims. Relying parties validate signatures, issuer, audience, nonce, expiry and other protocol properties before trusting identity information.
offensiveRelevance: Testing commonly examines redirect handling, nonce and state, token validation, signing algorithms, issuer confusion, discovery metadata and claim trust.
defensiveRelevance: Validate ID tokens rigorously, restrict redirect URIs, use state and nonce correctly, prefer secure modern flows and avoid trusting unvalidated claims.

shortDefinition: A vulnerability where untrusted input changes the structure or meaning of a database query.
simpleExplanation: SQL injection happens when application input is treated as part of SQL syntax instead of being handled only as data.
technicalExplanation: The issue usually arises when dynamic SQL is built by concatenating untrusted input. Depending on the query context and database privileges, consequences can include unauthorised data access, modification, authentication bypass or broader database impact.
offensiveRelevance: Application security testing checks whether parameters can influence query logic, while keeping testing within authorised scope and impact constraints.
defensiveRelevance: Use parameterised queries or prepared statements, safe ORM APIs, least privilege database accounts, secure error handling and regression tests.

shortDefinition: A web attack that tricks an authenticated browser into performing an unintended action on a trusted application.
simpleExplanation: CSRF abuses the fact that a browser automatically sends a user’s existing authentication state with requests to a trusted site.
technicalExplanation: If a state-changing endpoint does not verify request intent, attacker-controlled content can cause a logged-in browser to submit a request the user did not mean to make.
offensiveRelevance: Testing checks whether sensitive state-changing requests require unpredictable anti-CSRF tokens, origin validation or step-up authentication.
defensiveRelevance: Use anti-CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies, origin checks and re-authentication for sensitive actions.

shortDefinition: An access-control weakness where changing an object reference can expose another user’s data or resources.
simpleExplanation: An application trusts an object identifier without checking whether the requester is allowed to access that object.
technicalExplanation: IDOR occurs when object-level authorisation is missing or inconsistent for identifiers in URLs, parameters, API bodies or path segments.
offensiveRelevance: Testing checks whether object references can be modified to access resources belonging to another user or role.
defensiveRelevance: Enforce server-side object-level authorisation for every request and every referenced resource.

shortDefinition: A vulnerability in unsafe XML parsing that can resolve external entities and expose local or internal resources.
simpleExplanation: An unsafe XML parser may follow external references supplied by an attacker.
technicalExplanation: XXE arises when a parser processes DTDs and external entities from untrusted XML. This can lead to local file disclosure, SSRF or denial of service depending on parser capabilities.
offensiveRelevance: Testing checks parser behaviour with external entities and DTD processing while limiting impact.
defensiveRelevance: Disable external entities and DTD processing, use hardened parsers and validate input formats.

shortDefinition: A vulnerability where untrusted input is interpreted by a server-side template engine as template syntax.
simpleExplanation: User-controlled text is evaluated by a template engine instead of being displayed only as data.
technicalExplanation: SSTI occurs when templates or template expressions are built from untrusted input. Depending on the engine and sandbox, this can expose application objects or enable server-side execution.
offensiveRelevance: Testing identifies template expression evaluation and determines the reachable template context without unnecessary impact.
defensiveRelevance: Keep templates static, treat user input as data, use safe rendering APIs and restrict template engine capabilities.

shortDefinition: A vulnerability where untrusted input becomes part of an operating-system command executed by the server.
simpleExplanation: The application passes attacker-controlled data into a shell or system command without safe separation.
technicalExplanation: OS command injection typically occurs when applications concatenate untrusted input into shell commands or invoke unsafe process APIs.
offensiveRelevance: Testing determines whether input can alter intended command execution while keeping validation controlled and non-destructive.
defensiveRelevance: Avoid shell execution, use parameter-safe process APIs, strict allowlists, least privilege and monitoring.

shortDefinition: A file-access vulnerability where manipulated paths escape the intended directory.
simpleExplanation: Directory traversal happens when an application accepts a file path and does not safely constrain it to the intended directory.
technicalExplanation: Path traversal commonly involves path sequences or alternate encodings that cause path resolution outside an allowed base directory. Impact depends on application privileges and reachable files.
offensiveRelevance: Application assessments verify whether file-related parameters can escape the intended directory boundary.
defensiveRelevance: Use canonical path validation, allowlisted identifiers, fixed base directories, least privilege and avoid exposing raw filesystem paths.

shortDefinition: Unsafe handling of untrusted serialized data that can alter application behaviour or trigger unintended code paths.
simpleExplanation: The application rebuilds objects from data it does not fully trust, allowing crafted data to influence object state or behaviour.
technicalExplanation: Risk appears when untrusted serialized objects are deserialized with powerful object types, gadget chains or insufficient type restrictions.
offensiveRelevance: Testing focuses on whether user-controlled serialized data reaches unsafe deserialization code paths.
defensiveRelevance: Prefer simple data formats, restrict allowed types, validate integrity, avoid unsafe native deserialization and run with least privilege.
owasp: A08:2021 Software and Data Integrity Failures

shortDefinition: The practices and controls used to protect APIs from unauthorised access, abuse and data exposure.
simpleExplanation: API security ensures that only the right identities can call the right endpoints with valid input and appropriate permissions.
technicalExplanation: Core controls include strong authentication, object- and function-level authorisation, schema validation, rate limiting, secure defaults, logging and careful data exposure.
offensiveRelevance: API assessments examine authentication, authorisation, object access, input validation, business logic and excessive data exposure.
defensiveRelevance: Enforce server-side access control, validate schemas, use least privilege, rate limits, inventory endpoints and monitor abuse.

shortDefinition: An authentication relay technique where captured NTLM authentication is forwarded to another service.
simpleExplanation: Instead of cracking a password, an adversary forwards a victim's NTLM authentication exchange to a service that accepts it.
technicalExplanation: Relay becomes possible when NTLM is accepted without protections such as SMB signing, LDAP signing or channel binding, and when the target service authorises the relayed identity.
offensiveRelevance: AD assessments use relay scenarios to validate authentication hardening and service protections.
defensiveRelevance: Require SMB and LDAP signing where applicable, enable channel binding, reduce NTLM use and monitor unusual authentication paths.

shortDefinition: Microsoft's enterprise PKI role for issuing and managing certificates in Active Directory environments.
simpleExplanation: AD CS lets organisations issue certificates for users, computers and services, but unsafe templates or permissions can create powerful identity risks.
technicalExplanation: Security depends on certificate template configuration, enrollment permissions, issuance requirements, EKUs, CA protections and certificate-based authentication paths.
offensiveRelevance: AD assessments review certificate templates and enrollment paths for misconfigurations that could allow unintended authentication or privilege escalation.
defensiveRelevance: Harden templates, restrict enrollment rights, require appropriate approvals, protect CA systems and monitor certificate issuance.

shortDefinition: A Windows application control technology that uses rules to allow or block executables, scripts, installers and packaged apps.
simpleExplanation: AppLocker helps organisations control which applications and scripts users are allowed to run on Windows systems.
technicalExplanation: AppLocker evaluates rule collections such as Executable, Script, Windows Installer and Packaged App rules using publisher, path and file hash conditions, with enforcement or audit modes.
offensiveRelevance: Security assessments review effective AppLocker policy, trusted paths and rule gaps to understand the execution boundary.
defensiveRelevance: Use least privilege, minimise writable trusted paths, prefer publisher or hash rules where appropriate, audit changes and monitor blocked execution events.

shortDefinition: A Windows interface that lets applications submit script and content data to antimalware products for inspection.
simpleExplanation: AMSI gives security products visibility into content handled by applications such as PowerShell and scripting hosts before or during execution.
technicalExplanation: AMSI exposes content scanning APIs that supported applications call so registered antimalware providers can inspect script blocks or other dynamic content and return a verdict.
offensiveRelevance: Assessments validate whether script content is visible to endpoint security controls and how detection layers interact.
defensiveRelevance: Keep the antimalware provider healthy, monitor AMSI-related detections, combine with application control and use constrained administrative workflows.

shortDefinition: An Active Directory capability that allows a trusted service to access another service on behalf of a user.
simpleExplanation: Delegation lets one service represent a user to another service when that behaviour is explicitly configured.
technicalExplanation: Active Directory supports unconstrained, constrained and resource-based constrained delegation. Security depends on SPN configuration, delegation rights, protocol transition settings and protected accounts.
offensiveRelevance: AD assessments enumerate delegation relationships because over-permissive configurations can create privilege and lateral movement paths.
defensiveRelevance: Prefer constrained models, restrict delegation rights, protect privileged accounts, review SPNs and monitor unusual service-ticket activity.

shortDefinition: A Unix permission bit that causes an executable to run with the effective user ID of its owner.
simpleExplanation: SUID is often used for legitimate administrative helpers, but unsafe SUID programs can create privilege-escalation risk.
technicalExplanation: When the SUID bit is set on an executable, the process effective UID becomes the file owner during execution. Risk depends on ownership, program behaviour, environment handling and input validation.
offensiveRelevance: Linux assessments inventory SUID binaries and review unusual or writable programs for privilege-boundary weaknesses.
defensiveRelevance: Remove unnecessary SUID bits, keep privileged binaries patched, restrict writable locations and monitor permission changes.

shortDefinition: Insecure Kubernetes settings or permissions that expose workloads, credentials or cluster control paths.
simpleExplanation: Kubernetes becomes risky when access, networking, secrets or workload policies are configured too broadly.
technicalExplanation: Common risk areas include exposed APIs, excessive RBAC, privileged containers, weak network policies, insecure secrets handling and permissive admission or workload settings.
offensiveRelevance: Cloud assessments review cluster exposure, RBAC, service accounts, workloads, network boundaries and secret access for unintended paths.
defensiveRelevance: Apply least-privilege RBAC, restrict API access, use network policies, harden workloads, protect secrets and enforce admission controls.
